passages.source_text: Νύκτωρ δὲ διαναστὰς καὶ διυπνίσας ἡμᾶς, καθεσθεὶς συνήθως ἔφη Πυνθάνεσθέ μου περὶ ὧν βούλεσθε. καὶ ὁ Σοφονίας αὐτῷ πρῶτος ἤρξατο Πῶς ὄντως ὁ περὶ πονηροῦ λόγος ἔχει, ἐπιθυμοῦσιν ἡμῖν μαθεῖν ὑφήγησαι. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἤδη μέν, ἔφη, καὶ διὰ τῆς πρὸς Σίμωνα διαλέξεως ἐξέφηνα, τῷ δὲ σὺν ἑτέροις κεφαλαίοις τὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ εἰρηκέναι οὐ πάνυ σαφῶς ἐφωτίσθη. πολλὰ γὰρ κεφάλαια ἰσοδυναμεῖν δοκοῦντα τῷ ἀληθεῖ αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἀληθοῦς τοῖς πλείοσι παρέχει τινὰ γνῶσιν· ὥστε, ἐὰν νῦν ὑμῖν εἴπω ἃ τότε μετὰ πολλῶν εἰρήκειν κεφαλαίων τῷ Σίμωνι, μὴ οἰηθῆτε ἴσῃ αὐτῷ τιμῇ τετιμῆσθαι. καὶ ὁ Σοφονίας Ὀρθῶς, ἔφη, λέγεις· εἰ νῦν γὰρ ἡμῖν ἐκ πολλῶν τῶν τότε εἰρημένων κεφαλαίων ἀφορίζεις, αὐτὸ τὸ ἀληθὲς ποιήσεις φανερώτερον.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἀκούσατε, ἔφη, τοιγαροῦν τῆς περὶ τοῦ πονηροῦ ἁρμονίας τὴν ἀλήθειαν. ὁ θεὸς δύο βασιλείας ὁρίσας καὶ δύο αἰῶνας συνεστήσατο, κρίνας τῷ πονηρῷ δεδόσθαι τὸν παρόντα κόσμον διὰ τὸ μικρόν τε αὐτὸν εἶναι καὶ παρέρχεσθαι ὀξέως, τῷ δὲ ἀγαθῷ δώσειν ὑπέσχετο τὸν μέλλοντα αἰῶνα, ἅτε δὴ μέγαν ὄντα καὶ ἀΐδιον. τὸν οὖν ἄνθρωπον αὐτεξούσιον ἐποίησεν, ἐπιτηδειότητα ἔχοντα νεύειν πρὸς ἃς βούλεται πράξεις. καὶ τὸ μὲν σῶμα αὐτοῦ ἐστὶ τριμερές, ἐκ θηλείας ἔχον τὴν γένεσιν· ἔχει γὰρ ἐπιθυμίαν, ὀργήν, λύπην καὶ τὰ τούτοις ἑπόμενα — τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα (καὶ αὐτὸ οὐ τριτογενὲς ὄν, ἀλλὰ τριμερές) ἐκ τοῦ ἄρρενος ἔχει τὴν γένεσιν καὶ δεκτικόν ἐστι λογισμοῦ, γνώσεως, φόβου καὶ τῶν τούτοις ἑπομένων. ἑκατέρα δὲ τῶν τριάδων μίαν ἔχει τὴν ῥίζαν, ὡς εἶναι τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐκ φυραμάτων δύο, θηλείας τε καὶ ἄρρενος. διὸ δὴ καὶ δύο αὐτῷ ὁδοὶ προετέθησαν, νόμου τε καὶ ἀνομίας — δύο τε βασιλεῖαι ὡρίσθησαν, ἡ μὲν οὐρανῶν λεγομένη, ἡ δὲ τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς νῦν βασιλευόντων. ἀλλὰ καὶ δύο βασιλεῖς ἐτάχθησαν, ὧν ὁ μὲν τοῦ παρόντος καὶ προσκαίρου κόσμου νόμῳ βασιλεύειν χειροτονεῖται, ὃς καὶ ἐπ’ ὀλέθρῳ πονηρῶν χαίρειν ἐκράθη — ὁ δὲ ἕτερος, καὶ αὐτὸς βασιλεὺς ὑπάρχων (τοῦ ἐσομένου αἰῶνος), στέργει πᾶσαν ἀνθρώπων φύσιν, ἐν τοῖς παροῦσι τὴν παρρησίαν ἔχειν οὐ δυνάμενος ..... ὧς, τίς ποτ’ ἔστι λανθάνειν πειρώμενος τὰ συμφέροντα συμβουλεύει.

τῶν δὲ δύο τούτων ..... τὸν ἕτερον ἐκβιάζεται, θεοῦ κελεύσαντος. ἕκαστος δὲ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐξουσίαν ἔχει........... ὥ αὐτῶν ᾧ βούλεται πείθεσθαι πρὸς τὸ πράσσειν ἀγαθὰ ἢ κακά· πλὴν ἐὰν τὰ ἀγαθά τις πράσσειν ἕληται, τοῦ ἐσομένου ἀγαθοῦ βασιλέως γίνεται κτῆμα — εἰ δὲ φαῦλα πράξειέ τις, τοῦ παρόντος γίνεται πονηροῦ ὑπηρέτημα, ὃς δι’ ἁμαρτίας κρίσει δικαίᾳ τὴν κατ’ αὐτοῦ λαβὼν ἐξουσίαν καὶ πρὸ τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος θελήσας ἐν τῷ νῦν βίῳ κολάζων ἥδεται καὶ ὡς ἰδίᾳ χαριζόμενος ἐπιθυμίᾳ τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ βούλησιν ἐκτελεῖ. ὁ δὲ ἕτερος ἐπὶ δικαίων ἐξουσίᾳ χαίρειν δημιουργηθείς, δίκαιον εὑρὼν μεγάλως εὐφραίνεται, σώζων αὐτὸν ἀϊδίῳ ζωῇ, καὶ αὐτὸς δὲ ὡς ἑαυτῷ χαριζόμενος, τὴν ὑπὲρ τούτων εἰς θεὸν ἀναφέρει χάριν. ἔξεστι δὲ παντὶ ἀδίκῳ μεταμεληθέντι σώζεσθαι καὶ παντὶ δικαίῳ ἀνδρὶ ἐπὶ τελευταίας ἁμαρτίας δίκην ὑπέχειν. πλὴν οἱ δύο ἡγεμόνες οὗτοι ταχεῖαι χεῖρές εἰσι θεοῦ προλαμβάνειν ἐπιθυμοῦσαι τὸ αὐτοῦ θέλημα ἐπιτελεῖν. ὅτι δὲ τοῦθ’ οὕτως ἔχει, εἴρηται καὶ τῷ νόμῳ ἐκ προσώπου τοῦ θεοῦ „ἐγὼ ἀποκτενῶ καὶ ζῆν ποιήσω, πατάξω κἀγὼ ἰάσομαι“. ἀληθῶς γὰρ ἀποκτέννει καὶ ζωοποιεῖ, ἀποκτέννει μὲν διὰ τῆς ἀριστερᾶς, τουτέστι διὰ τοῦ ἐπὶ κακώσει τῶν ἀσεβῶν χαίρειν κραθέντος πονηροῦ — σώζει δὲ καὶ εὐεργετεῖ διὰ τῆς δεξιᾶς, τουτέστι διὰ τοῦ ἐπ’ εὐεργεσίᾳ καὶ σωτηρίᾳ δικαίων χαίρειν δημιουργηθέντος ἀγαθοῦ. εἰσὶ δὲ οὗτοι τὰς οὐσίας ἔχοντες οὐκ ἔξωθεν τοῦ θεοῦ· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔστιν ἑτέρα τις ἀρχή. οὐ μὴν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ὡς ζῷα προεβλήθησαν (ὁμόδοξοι γὰρ αὐτῷ ἦσαν) οὔτε συμβεβήκασιν, αὐτομάτως παρὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ βουλὴν γεγονότες (ἐπεὶ τὸ τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ μέγιστον ἀνῄρητο ἄν), ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ μὲν προβέβληνται τὰ πρώτιστα στοιχεῖα τέσσαρα, τό τε θερμὸν καὶ ψυχρὸν ὑγρόν τε καὶ ξηρόν. ὅθεν δὴ καὶ πατὴρ τυγχάνει πάσης οὐσίας ..... οὔσης γνώμης τῆς μετὰ τὴν κρᾶσιν· ἔξω γὰρ κραθεῖσιν αὐτοῖς ὡς τέκνον ἡ προαίρεσις ἐγεννήθη. ὁ οὖν πονηρὸς πρὸς τῷ τοῦ ἐνεστῶτος κόσμου τέλει ὑπουργήσας ἀμέμπτως τῷ θεῷ, ἅτε δὴ οὐ μιᾶς οὐσίας ὢν τῆς πρὸς κακίαν μονῆς μετασυγκριθεὶς ἀγαθὸς γενέσθαι δύναται. οὐδὲ γὰρ νῦν κακόν τι ποιεῖ, καίτοι κακὸς ὤν, νομίμως κακουχεῖν εἰληφὼς τὴν ἐξουσίαν.

ταῦτα τοῦ Πέτρου εἰπόντος, Μιχαίας, καὶ αὐτὸς τῶν ἀκολούθων τις ὤν, ἐπύθετο Πόθεν οὖν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τὸ ἁμαρτάνειν; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ἐκ τοῦ ἀγνοεῖν ὅτι περὶ ὧν πράσσουσι κακῶς κρί[σεως γε]νομένης πάντως κολασθῆναι ἔχουσιν· ὅθεν καὶ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν (ὡς ἄλλοτε εἶ[πον]) [εἰς] διαδοχὴν βίου ἔχοντες, ταύτην πληροφοροῦσιν ὡς ἔτυχεν, ἤμ[ιπεπείρων] παίδων φθορᾷ ἢ ἄλλῃ τινὶ κολακευούσῃ ἁμαρτίᾳ. τῷ γὰρ ἀγνοεῖν ὅτι κρίνονται (ὡς φθάσας εἶπον) διὰ τὸ ἄφοβον τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν οὐ νομίμως πληροῦν ἐπείγονται. ὥστε οὐχ ὁ θεὸς κακός, ὁ καλῶς θεὶς τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἵνα διαδοχὴ βίου γένηται, ἀλλ’ αὐτοὶ ἀσεβέστατοι, οἱ τῷ καλῷ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας χρησάμενοι κακῶς. οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ὀργῆς ἔστι λογίσασθαι ὅτι δικαίως μὲν αὐτῇ τις χρησάμενος ὡς ἔξεστιν, εὐσεβεῖ — παρὰ δὲ τὸ μέτρον ἐξελθὼν καὶ ἑαυτῷ τὴν κρίσιν λαβὼν ἀσεβεῖ.

καὶ ὁ Σοφονίας πάλιν ἔφη Ἡ μακροθυμία σου, κύριέ μου Πέτρε, παρρησίαν ἡμῖν χαρίζεται ἀκριβείας χάριν κατὰ πολλὰ πυνθάνεσθαί σου· διὸ θαρροῦντες παντὶ τρόπῳ τὴν ἐξέτασιν ποιούμεθα. μέμνημαι τοίνυν ὡς χθὲς Σίμων πρὸς σὲ τὴν ζήτησιν ἔχων ἔφη ὅτι ὁ πονηρός, εἰ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ γεγέννηται, ἀκολούθως τῆς αὐτῆς τῷ προβαλόντι τυγχάνει οὐσίας καὶ ἀγαθὸς ὤφειλεν εἶναι καὶ οὐχὶ κακός. σὺ δὲ ἀπεκρίνω μὴ πάντως οὕτως ἔχειν, καθότι πολλοὶ ἐξ ἀγαθῶν κακοὶ γεννῶνται, ὥσπερ ἐκ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ ἀνόμοιοί τινες ὄντες δύο ἐγεννήθησαν, ὧν ὁ μὲν ἦν κακός, ὁ δ’ ἀγαθός. τοῦ δὲ Σίμωνος αἰτιασαμένου ὅτι ἀνθρωπίνοις ἐχρήσω παραδείγμασιν, ἀπεκρίνω ὅτι τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ οὐδὲ τὸ γεννῆσαι θεὸν παραδέξασθαι δεῖ· ἀνθρώπινον γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο τὸ παράδειγμα. ἐγὼ δὲ Σοφονίας τὸ μὲν γεννῆσαι θεὸν παραδέχομαι, τὸ δὲ κακὸν γεννῆσαι οὐ προσίεμαι, κἂν τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ ἀγαθοὶ κακοὺς γεννῶσι. καὶ μήτοι νομίσῃς με ἀλόγως τῶν ἀνθρώποις διαφερόντων ἔνια μὲν τῷ θεῷ ἀποδιδόναι, ἔνια δὲ οὔ, ἐπειδὴ τὸ μὲν γεννῆσαι δίδωμι, τὸ δὲ ἀνόμοιον αὐτοῦ γεννῆσαι οὐκ ἀποδίδωμι. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄνθρωποι κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς ἀνομοίους ταῖς ἑαυτῶν γνώμαις γεννῶσιν υἱοὺς διὰ τοιαύτην αἰτίαν· ἐκ τεσσάρων γὰρ συνεστῶτες μερῶν κατὰ τὰς διαφόρους τροπὰς διαφόρως τρέπονται τὰ σώματα καὶ ὡς ἐν ἀνθρωπείῳ σώματι καθ’ ἕκαστον καιρὸν τὸ τῆς τροπῆς ἴδιον αὐξανόμενον ἢ ἐλαττούμενον τὴν σύμμετρον κρᾶσιν ἀθετεῖ. τῶν γὰρ συγκραμάτων οὐχ ὡσαύτως ἀεὶ διαμενόντων τὰ σπέρματα ἄλλοτε ἄλλην ἔχοντα κρᾶσιν ἀποκρίνονται, οἷς πρὸς τὴν τοῦ καιροῦ κρᾶσιν καὶ αἱ γνῶμαι ἕπονται εἴτε ἀγαθαὶ εἴτε κακαί. ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐκ ἔστι τι τοιοῦτον λογίσασθαι· ἄτρεπτον γὰρ καὶ ἀεὶ ὢν, ὅπ...... προβάλλειν βουληθείη, ἀνάγκη πᾶσα τὸ προβαλλόμενον αὐτῷ ὡσαύτως ...... τὰ πάντα τῷ γεγεννηκότι τήν τε οὐσίαν λέγω καὶ τὴν γνώμην. εἰ [δὲ θελήσ]ειέ τις καὶ αὐτὸν τρεπτὸν λέγειν, οὐκ οἶδα πῶς καὶ ἀθάνατον εἰπεῖν δύναται αὐτόν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table

passages.text: During the night, he rose, woke us, and sat down as usual. He said, “Ask me about whatever you wish.” Sophonias was the first to begin with him: “Since we desire to learn, explain to us how the account concerning the evil one truly stands.” Peter said, “I have indeed already made it clear through the discussion with Simon, but because the things concerning him were stated together with other points, the matter was not brought to light very clearly. For many points that seem equal in force to the truth give most people some knowledge of the truth itself. Therefore, if I now tell you what I had then told Simon among many points, do not suppose that you have been honored equally with him.” Sophonias said, “You speak rightly. For if you now separate it out for us from the many points stated then, you will make the actual truth clearer.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective is substantival and contextually denotes the personal evil ruler discussed in the following sections; “evil” as an abstraction is a possible broader alternative.
The word denotes principal points, headings, or topics in an argument.
In the warning about equal honor, the pronoun most naturally refers to Simon. A reference to the subject matter is less consistent with Sophonias’s reply.
The verb means to distinguish or set apart; its unstated object is contextually the matter under discussion.

passages.text: Peter said, “Hear, therefore, the truth about the ordering concerning the evil one. God defined two kingdoms and constituted two ages. He decided that the present world was to be given to the evil one because it is small and passes away quickly, but he promised to give the coming age to the good one, since it is great and eternal. He therefore made the human being self-determining, with the capacity to incline toward whatever actions he wishes. His body is three-part and has its origin from the female, for it has desire, anger, grief, and the things that follow these. The spirit—though itself not third in origin but three-part—has its origin from the male and is receptive to reasoning, knowledge, fear, and the things that follow these. Each of the two triads has one root, so that the human being is from two compounds, female and male. For this reason two ways were also set before him, that of law and that of lawlessness. Two kingdoms were also defined: one called the kingdom of the heavens, and the other the kingdom of those now reigning upon the earth. Moreover, two kings were appointed. One is appointed by law to reign over the present and temporary world, and he was blended so as to delight in the destruction of the wicked. The other, himself also being king of the age that is to come, loves the whole human race. Unable in the present circumstances to have freedom to speak openly ..... as, while trying to conceal who he is, he counsels what is beneficial.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can denote an arrangement, composition, or harmonious ordering. “Ordering” suits the ensuing account of paired ages, kingdoms, rulers, and elemental mixtures.
The term describes possessing authority over one’s own choices, not unlimited power.
The contrast distinguishes being third-generated or third in derivation from being three-part. “Third-born” is a more literal alternative.
The word evokes kneaded masses or mixtures and supports the author’s composite anthropology.
The verb denotes selection or appointment; the accompanying reference to law presents the rule as authorized.
The compositional force is retained because the following section explains the rulers through elemental blending.
The noun can mean boldness, freedom of speech, or openness. The following effort to remain concealed favors open speech or action.
The infinitive describes escaping notice. Here it is understood as concealing the king’s identity; “to remain unnoticed” is also possible.

passages.text: “Of these two ..... compels the other, at God’s command. Each person has authority ........... by which to obey whichever of them he wishes, for the purpose of doing good or evil. If someone chooses to do good things, he becomes the possession of the good king who is to come. But if someone should do base things, he becomes an instrument of the present evil one. Through sin, the latter has received authority over him by a just judgment; and, wishing to do so even before the coming age, he delights in punishing him in the present life and, as one gratifying his own desire, carries out God’s will. The other was created to delight in exercising authority over righteous people. When he finds a righteous person, he rejoices greatly, saving him by eternal life; and he too, as one gratifying himself, offers God thanks for them. Every unjust person may be saved after regretting his course, and every righteous man may incur punishment for a final sin. But these two rulers are God’s swift hands, desiring to act beforehand in accomplishing his will. That this is so is also stated in the law in the person of God: ‘I will kill and make alive; I will strike, and I too will heal.’ For he truly kills and gives life. He kills through the left hand, that is, through the evil one who was blended so as to delight in the affliction of the impious. But he saves and benefits through the right hand, that is, through the good one who was created to delight in benefiting and saving the righteous. These have their substances not from outside God, for there is no other first principle. Yet they were not brought forth by God as living beings, for then they would have shared his disposition. Nor did they arise accidentally, having come into being spontaneously contrary to his purpose, since then the greatest part of his power would have been abolished. Rather, the four primary elements were brought forth from God: hot and cold, wet and dry. Thus he is indeed the father of every substance ..... disposition being what comes after the blending; for when they were blended outside, choice was born as their offspring. At the end of the present world, therefore, the evil one, after serving God blamelessly, can, since he is not of a single substance, become good when recomposed away from persistence in evil. For even now he does nothing evil, although he is evil, since he has lawfully received authority to inflict suffering.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The form is taken as a dative relative whose antecedent may have stood in the preceding lacuna. An erroneous or incomplete construction is also possible.
The word denotes something acquired or owned and presents the person as belonging to the coming good king.
The formation denotes something that serves or ministers. “Servant” is possible, but “instrument” preserves its contrast with “possession.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: and, as one gratifying his own desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction with ὡς presents the action under the description of gratifying his own desire while he fulfills God’s will. “As though gratifying his own desire” is also possible, but need not imply that the gratification is unreal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and he too, as one gratifying himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: This parallel ὡς construction characterizes the good ruler’s action as self-gratification. The alternative “as though gratifying himself” is possible but does not necessarily deny actual gratification.
The verb can denote regret, reconsideration, or a change of mind. The context entails departure from injustice, but the distinct Greek terminology is preserved rather than homogenized.
The adjective may describe one last sin or a sin committed at the end of life; the rendering leaves both temporal nuances possible.
The author’s bodily image for the two rulers is preserved rather than reduced to “agents.”
The verb conveys anticipation or acting in advance; the rulers perform divine punishment or benefit before final judgment.
The adjective means sharing the same opinion or disposition, not possessing the same glory.
The adverb is retained without an invented object. It may mean outside God or externally to the original divine bringing-forth.

The participle denotes recomposition or alteration by mixture. The following genitive is taken as separation from persistence in evil; alternatively, that genitive may characterize a hypothetical single substance fixed in evil.
The verb describes subjecting others to hardship or maltreatment; the author presents that activity as lawfully authorized punishment.

passages.text: After Peter said these things, Micaiah, who was also one of the followers, asked, “From where, then, does human sinning come?” Peter said, “It comes from not knowing that, when judgment has taken place concerning the things they do wrongly, they are certain to be punished. Consequently, although they possess desire for the continuation of life—as I said on another occasion—they satisfy it indiscriminately, through the corruption of half-mature boys or through some other pandering sin. Because they do not know that they are judged, as I said before, their lack of fear drives them to satisfy desire unlawfully. Thus God is not evil, for he established desire well so that there might be continuation of life. Rather, they themselves are most impious, since they have used what is good in desire badly. The same reasoning may also be applied to anger: someone who uses it justly, as is permitted, acts piously, but one who goes beyond the proper measure and takes judgment upon himself acts impiously.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive denotes committing wrong or sin; the question asks for its source.
The term refers to succession or perpetuation, here the continuation of human life through generation.
Here the verb describes bringing desire to fulfillment rather than intellectual assurance.
The editorially marked adjective portrays the boys as only partly mature, literally half-ripened.
The participle portrays the sin as flattering or catering to desire; “enticing” is another possible rendering.
The wording distinguishes desire’s good divinely assigned function from its wrongful human use.

The phrase may mean that the person takes judgment into his own hands by assuming authority to judge or punish, which fits the discussion of exceeding the proper use of anger. It may instead mean that he incurs or receives judgment for himself, which fits the preceding emphasis on being judged and punished. The English intentionally leaves both readings available.

passages.text: Sophonias spoke again: “Your patience, my lord Peter, grants us boldness to ask you questions on many points for the sake of precision. Therefore, taking courage, we conduct the examination in every way. I remember, then, that yesterday, while Simon was engaged in inquiry with you, he said that if the evil one was generated from God, it follows that he shares the same substance as the one who brought him forth and ought to have been good, not evil. You answered that this does not necessarily follow, since many evil people are born from good people. In the same way, two individuals unlike each other were born from Adam, one of whom was evil and the other good. When Simon objected that you had used human examples, you answered that by this reasoning one should not accept that God begets either, for this too is a human example. But I, Sophonias, accept that God begets; I do not accept that he begets evil, even if good people among human beings beget evil ones. And do not suppose that I irrationally ascribe to God some things pertaining to human beings but not others, because I concede begetting to him but do not ascribe to him the begetting of what is unlike him. Human beings naturally beget sons whose dispositions are unlike their own for the following reason: because they are composed of four parts, their bodies change in different ways according to different alterations; and in a human body, as the distinctive quality of the alteration at each particular time increases or decreases, it disrupts the proportionate mixture. Because the compounds do not always remain the same, the seeds are secreted at different times with different mixtures, and dispositions, whether good or evil, follow them in accordance with the mixture at that time. But in God’s case no such thing can be conceived, for since he is unchangeable and always existent, wh...... he might wish to bring forth, it is altogether necessary that what is brought forth by him should likewise ...... in every respect in relation to the one who begot it—I mean both substance and disposition. But if anyone should wish to call even him changeable, I do not know how he can also call him immortal.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes forbearance or patience, here Peter’s willingness to endure extensive questioning.
Here the noun denotes confidence or freedom to question Peter openly.
The adverb marks Simon’s inference that what comes from God must share God’s substance and goodness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who brought him forth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes derivation or production without requiring the more technical English term “emanated.”
The contrast between the evil and good sons favors mutual dissimilarity, though the phrase could instead mean that both differed from Adam in some respect.
In context the participle concerns features found among or associated with human beings. “Things in which human beings differ” is grammatically possible but fits the argument less well.
The term denotes changes or turnings, possibly including seasonal or elemental variations.
The phrase denotes the quality or component proper to a particular bodily alteration, likely one of the elemental qualities.
The verb has the physiological sense of being separated or secreted in the discussion of bodily seed.
The adjective directly contrasts God with the changing bodily mixtures described immediately beforehand.
Here the noun denotes disposition, purpose, or cast of mind. “Opinion” is possible but too narrow for the contrast between good and evil offspring.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
